WAHIDI-BASIT:v24p235#2/r9.claim: Al-Azharī takes camel dabḥ as dabʿ, stretching the forelegs; Abū ʿUbaydah treats the two words as equivalent.

WAHIDI-QT:100:1/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-QT:100:1/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-QT:100:1/r1.claim: The chargers are horses in battle, panting with the sound of their insides while running.

WAHIDI-WAJIZ:100:1-8/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:100:1-8/r1.speaker: author
WAHIDI-WAJIZ:100:1-8/r1.claim: The chargers are horses on raids; dabḥ is the sound of their insides as they run.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r1.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r1.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r1.claim: The initial wāw is an oath; al-ʿādiyāt is the feminine sound plural active participle of ʿadw, meaning to run or race quickly.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r2.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r2.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r2.claim: The term can refer to horses, camels, or any running creatures.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r3.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r3.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r3.claim: As Besāʾir explains, the root ʿadw fundamentally means crossing or exceeding a limit; considered as movement, it gives ʿadw, running.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r4.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r4.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r4.claim: Considered as an inward disposition, the root yields ʿadāwa and muʿādāt, hostility.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r5.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r5.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r5.claim: Considered as injustice, the root yields ʿudwān, oppression and transgression.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r6.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r6.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r6.claim: Considered spatially, the root yields ʿadwā, contagion; the other meanings derive from these senses.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r7.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r7.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r7.claim: In battle usage, ʿadī and ʿādiya name troops that habitually rush to attack.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r8.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r8.speaker: Bazıları
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r8.claim: Some restrict ʿadī to attacking infantry and ʿādiya to attacking cavalry.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r9.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r9.speaker: Hazret-i Ali
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r9.claim: A report from Ali interprets the runners as pilgrims’ camels going to Arafat.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r10.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r10.speaker: İbn Abbas
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r10.claim: Ibn Abbas’s report identifies them as cavalry horses; Elmalılı says this is clear from the verses and is the choice of most exegetes.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r11.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r11.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r11.claim: Dabḥ is the sound of horses’ rapid breathing while running, a huff.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r12.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r12.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r12.claim: This breathing is distinct from neighing and from the sound horses make on seeing food or their owner.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r13.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r13.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r13.claim: Some say dabḥ occurs when either a horse or a dog runs.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r14.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r14.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r14.claim: The phrase can be parsed as taḍbaḥu ḍabḥan or as dābiḥāt.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r19.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r19.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r19.claim: Those who read al-ʿādiyāt as pilgrims’ camels also explain al-mūriyāt as pilgrims who travel at night from Arafat to Muzdalifa and light a fire at the Sacred Monument.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r23.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r23.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r23.claim: Elmalılı extends the image to modern fire-sparking weapons literally and, by extension, fast motorized assault vehicles; a Meccan dating, when Muslims had neither horses nor weapons, would make the future reference especially clear.

ELMALILI:100:1-2/r24.author: Elmalılı Muhammed Hamdi Yazır
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r24.speaker: author
ELMALILI:100:1-2/r24.claim: The distinctive plural forms and successive faʾs suggest an ordered development of attack vehicles through the ages, encompassing motorized raiders as well as horses.

KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:100:1/r1.author: Hayreddin Karaman, Mustafa Çağrıcı, İbrahim Kâfi Dönmez, Sadrettin Gümüş
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:100:1/r1.speaker: author
KURANYOLU-TEFSIR:100:1/r1.claim: The oath depicts horses charging the enemy in battle, then swears by them because after humans they were the most important element of old warfare. It points to God as the giver of these useful, much-loved possessions and uses what people valued to stress the truth and importance of the following message.

SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p234/r1.author: al-Suyūṭī
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p234/r1.speaker: ابن عباس
SUYUTI-LUBAB:v1p234/r1.claim: Al-Bazzar, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Hakim report from Ibn Abbas that the Prophet sent out horses; after a month without news, this verse was revealed.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p463/r1.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p463/r1.speaker: مقاتل
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p463/r1.claim: Muqatil says the Prophet sent an expedition against a clan of Kinana under al-Mundhir ibn Amr al-Ansari; when news was delayed, hypocrites claimed all had been killed, so God revealed the horses in this verse.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p463/r2.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p463/r2.speaker: ابن عباس
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p463/r2.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that the Messenger sent horses which ranged far for a month without news reaching him; the verse and the rest of the sura were then revealed, describing their nostril-breathing.

WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p463/r3.author: al-Wāḥidī
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p463/r3.speaker: author
WAHIDI-ASBAB:v1p463/r3.claim: Wahidi explains ashabat as traveling far across wide open plains; sahb is the singular of suhūb, meaning broad land.
